name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q01 - Outcome of meiosis in diploid organisms

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Meiosis is a specialized reductional cell division essential for sexually reproducing diploid organisms. It comprises two successive nuclear divisions following a single cycle of DNA replication.

Step 2: Evaluation of Outcomes
First, meiosis produces haploid gametes required for sexual reproduction.
Second, it halves the chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n), ensuring that upon fertilization the diploid number is restored.
Third, crossing over during pachytene of prophase I and random independent assortment of maternal and paternal chromosomes during metaphase I introduce genetic variations in the resulting progeny.

Step 3: Conclusion
All of the listed outcomes—production of gametes, reduction in chromosome number, and introduction of variation—result from meiosis in diploid organisms. Hence, the comprehensive conclusion encompassing all these effects is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q02 - Final determination of gamete genetic constitution

questiontext.text: At which stage of meiosis does the genetic constitution of gametes is finally decided

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The genetic identity and chromosomal makeup of future gametes are determined by the segregation of maternal and paternal homologous chromosomes and the independent assortment of recombinant chromosomes.

Step 2: Analysis of Meiotic Stages
During anaphase I, homologous chromosome pairs separate from each other and move toward opposite poles. Because each pole receives a randomly segregated set of homologous chromosomes with their exchanged genetic segments (from crossing over), this physical separation irreversibly decides which alleles and parental homologs are segregated into each daughter cell nucleus. Subsequent division in meiosis II merely separates already segregated sister chromatids.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, the genetic constitution of the resulting gametes is finally decided during anaphase I.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q03 - Occurrence of meiosis during sexual reproduction

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Meiosis is a reduction division that halves the chromosome number to form haploid gametes or spores, which later fuse during syngamy to restore diploidy. Hence, meiosis is intrinsically coupled to the sexual cycle.

Step 2: Evaluation of Modes of Reproduction
Vegetative reproduction is a mode of asexual propagation that relies solely on mitotic cell divisions, generating offspring that are genetically identical clones of the parent plant without involving gametic reduction or syngamy. Consequently, meiosis does not take place in vegetative reproduction.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, meiosis occurs exclusively during sexual reproduction.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q04 - Separation of homologous chromosomes during anaphase

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Meiosis I is characterized by the reduction of chromosome number through the separation of paired homologous chromosomes, whereas sister chromatids remain physically united at their centromeres until meiosis II.

Step 2: Detailed Mechanism of Anaphase I
In anaphase I, shortening of kinetochore microtubules pulls the homologous partners of each bivalent apart to opposite spindle poles. The centromeres do not split at this stage, so sister chromatids remain attached together.

Step 3: Conclusion
Thus, anaphase I is specifically characterized by the separation of homologous chromosomes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q05 - Equal division as characteristic of mitosis

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cell division can be classified as either equational division or reductional division depending on whether the parental ploidy is maintained in the daughter cells.

Step 2: Features of Mitosis
Mitosis ensures that duplicated chromosomes are partitioned equally between two daughter nuclei, giving daughter cells identical chromosome number and genetic content relative to the parent cell. Hence, mitosis is defined as equal division (equational division). Reduction division and pairing of homologous chromosomes are unique hallmarks of meiosis.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, mitosis is characterised by equal division.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q06 - Structural components of a meiotic bivalent

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During zygotene of meiotic prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair together via synapsis to form a bivalent (also termed a tetrad due to its four chromatids).

Step 2: Counting Chromatids and Centromeres
A bivalent is formed by two homologous chromosomes. Each individual chromosome has already replicated during interphase and contains two sister chromatids held together at a single centromere. Thus, two homologous chromosomes together contain four chromatids and two centromeres.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, a bivalent of meiosis I consists of four chromatids and two centromeres.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q07 - Quiescent stage of non dividing cells

questiontext.text: Cells which are not dividing are likely to be at

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In multicellular organisms, certain cells exit the standard proliferative cell cycle and enter a specialized non-dividing state.

Step 2: Analysis of Cell Cycle Phases
Cells that do not divide further exit the G1 phase and enter an inactive, quiescent stage called G0 (G-zero). In this stage, cells remain metabolically active and carry out differentiated physiological functions, but do not undergo cell division unless specifically stimulated.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, cells that are not dividing are located at the G0 stage.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q08 - Absence of crossing over in mitosis

questiontext.text: Which of the events listed below is not observed during mitosis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mitosis is an equational division that preserves genetic stability and identical copies of chromosomes without recombining parental alleles.

Step 2: Comparison of Events
Chromatin condensation, migration of centrosomes/centrioles to opposite poles, and the appearance of condensed chromosomes with two sister chromatids joined at the centromere are all standard events of mitotic prophase. In contrast, crossing over involves reciprocal exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, an event that occurs strictly during the pachytene stage of prophase I in meiosis.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, crossing over is not observed during mitosis.

answer.text: Appearance of chromosomes with two chromatids joined together at the centromere.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q09 - Incorrect statement regarding cycles of meiosis

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Meiosis is characterized by two successive nuclear divisions (meiosis I and meiosis II), but involves only a single round of DNA replication during the pre-meiotic S phase.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statements
Pairing of homologous chromosomes occurs during zygotene of prophase I.
At the conclusion of meiosis, four haploid cells are formed.
The chromosome number in daughter cells is reduced to half of the parental value.
Only a single cycle of DNA replication occurs; there is no replication during interkinesis or prior to meiosis II.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, the statement claiming that two cycles of DNA replication occur is the wrong statement regarding meiosis.

answer.text: At the end of meiosis the number of chromosomes are reduced to half

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q10 - Characteristics of cell in gap phase

questiontext.text: Select the correct statement about G1 phase

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The G1 (gap 1) phase corresponds to the interval between mitosis and the initiation of DNA replication.

Step 2: Evaluation of G1 Characteristics
During the G1 phase, the cell is metabolically very active, continuously synthesizes RNA and proteins (macromolecules), and steadily grows in size. However, DNA replication has not yet begun; nuclear DNA replication takes place exclusively during the subsequent S (synthesis) phase. Thus, within G1, the DNA content remains unchanged and does not replicate.

Step 3: Conclusion
Therefore, the statement that DNA in the cell does not replicate is the correct statement about the G1 phase.

answer.text: DNA in the cell does not replicate
It is not a phase of synthesis of macromolecules
